meta.title: Art Forms, Art Tree | Many traditions. One living heritage.
meta.description: India's artistic traditions are as diverse as its landscapes, Gond Art, Phad, Pichwai, Sanjhi and Sohrai, each with a unique story and a living legacy.

hero.heading: Many traditions. One living heritage.
hero.lead: India's artistic traditions are as diverse as its landscapes and people, shaped by regions, communities, beliefs and ways of life. Each art form carries a unique story, a distinct visual language and a living legacy that continues to inspire.

artforms.title: Bhil
artforms.subtitle: Rajasthan · Madhya Pradesh · Gujarat · Forest keepers
artforms.excerpt: Bhil art is the visual tradition of one of India's oldest and largest tribal communities, the Bhils of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat, custodians of India's forests for aeons. Like most tribal peoples, the Bhils are pagan, their spirituality rooted not in scripture but in the living forces of nature. The defining characteristic of Bhil art is the dot: every surface, figures, animals, trees, borders, is covered in densely packed, carefully placed dots of endlessly varied colour.
modalParagraphs: Bhil art is the visual tradition of one of India's oldest and largest tribal communities, the Bhils of Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, custodians of India's forests for aeons. Like most tribal peoples, the Bhils are pagan, their spirituality rooted not in scripture but in the living forces of nature. Rain, sun, wind, the fertility of the earth, the turning of the seasons, each one a presence, each one honoured. This worldview is not the context for Bhil art. It is its very substance.

The defining characteristic of Bhil art is the dot. Every surface, figures, animals, trees, borders, backgrounds, is covered in densely packed, carefully placed dots of endlessly varied colour, each one applied with patient, deliberate intention.

The subjects of Bhil art are drawn directly from the world the Bhils inhabit and revere. Flora and fauna dominate, the trees, birds, animals, and rivers of the forest landscape rendered with the intimacy of a community that has lived among them for generations. Horses, peacocks, elephants, tigers, fish, flowering trees, the sun and moon, each one not merely depicted but honoured.

Local rituals and ceremonies fill the compositions alongside the natural world, festivals, harvests, marriages, and community gatherings specific to Bhil life and culture. These are not borrowed mythologies but living ones, rooted in a particular people and a particular place.

The Pithora painting deserves special mention, a large ceremonial work created collectively as an offering of gratitude to the deity Pithora Baba, painted on the walls of homes by specialist painters called Lakhara. A Pithora is not made, it is performed, the act of communal creation inseparable from the ritual it enacts.

artforms.title: Gond Art
artforms.subtitle: Madhya Pradesh · The Art of the Green Mountain
artforms.excerpt: Gond Art is the painting tradition of the Gond community of Central India, one of the subcontinent's largest and most ancient tribal peoples. The Gonds take their name from Kond, meaning 'the green mountain', and in that name lies the essence of this art: rooted in the earth, alive to nature, and convinced that the world is not merely material but inhabited at every level by spirit.
modalParagraphs: Gond Art is the painting tradition of the Gond community of Central India, one of the subcontinent's largest and most ancient tribal peoples. The Gonds take their name from Kond, meaning 'the green mountain', and in that name lies the essence of this art: rooted in the earth, alive to nature, and convinced that the world is not merely material but inhabited at every level by spirit.

The tradition has two original expressions, Bhitichitra, wall painting, and floor painting, both created on the surfaces of daily life as acts of ritual and devotion. At festivals, weddings, and auspicious occasions, homes were painted not for decoration but as offerings, a way of inviting the blessings of the natural world into the domestic space.

In the early 1980s, Jangarh Singh Shyam, a Gond artist from the village of Patangarh, translated this living tradition onto paper and canvas, giving it a new medium and a new name. The result was immediately recognised as something extraordinary: ancient and contemporary at once, rooted in one community's cosmology yet universally felt.

The visual grammar is instantly recognisable, bold double-lined outlines filled with densely packed dots, dashes, fish scales, and flowing lines that animate every surface from within. Birds, fish, elephants, trees, serpents, the creatures of the natural world, are rendered not as observed specimens but as living presences, each pulsing with inner life. To paint, in the Gond worldview, is to honour. To honour is to keep alive.

The tradition bears a striking resemblance to aboriginal art from Australia, two practices separated by an ocean, arriving independently at the same truth: that the dot, repeated with intention, can bring a surface to life.

Vibrant, mystical, and endlessly imaginative, Gond Art continues to grow, carried forward today by artists including Venkat Shyam, Ram Singh Urveti, and Bhajju Shyam, from the same green mountains that gave this tradition its name.

artforms.title: Madhubani
artforms.subtitle: Mithila, Bihar · The forest of honey
artforms.excerpt: Madhubani takes its name from the region that gave it birth, Madhu, honey, and Vana, forest, the forest of honey. Originating in the Mithila region of Bihar, Madhubani is among India's most ancient and most alive folk art traditions, traditionally practised solely by the women of the region. Legend holds that it was Raja Janak who first commissioned the painting of walls and floors to celebrate the wedding of Sita with Ram, giving birth to a tradition still alive today.
modalParagraphs: Madhubani painting takes its name from the region that gave it birth, Madhu, honey, and Vana, forest, the forest of honey. This name carries the sweetness and abundance this art has always celebrated. Originating in the Mithila region of Bihar, one of the oldest continuously inhabited regions of the Indian subcontinent, Madhubani is among India's most ancient and most alive folk art traditions. This art form was traditionally practised solely by women of the region.
Madhubani is not simply a folk tradition that happened to arise in Mithila. It is a tradition born in a royal household and practised by local folks, and for the most auspicious of all occasions.

Mithila was the kingdom of Raja Janak, Sita's father. Legend holds that it was Raja Janak who first commissioned the painting of walls and floors to celebrate the wedding of Sita with Ram. The women were asked to adorn every surface with auspicious images in honour of the occasion. In doing so, he gave birth to a tradition. The kohbar ghar, the bridal chamber, became the most sacred space for this art form. Its walls are still painted with the same devotion and the same imagery that were first invoked for Sita's own wedding night.

This is why Ram and Sita occupy the absolute centre of the Madhubani visual world. They are the reason the tradition exists, its presiding deities, and its eternal subject. Every Madhubani painting of a wedding, every kohbar ghar adorned for a bride, every lotus and fish and symbol of fertility, at some level, a remembrance of that first great celebration, the marriage of Ram and Sita in the kingdom of Mithila, painted into existence by the women of Janak's court, and never since forgotten.
Madhubani is not one tradition but five, each associated with a different community within the Mithila region, each with its own visual language and set of conventions.

Bharni — associated with the Brahmins, characterised by bold, filled forms. The subjects are primarily religious, gods, goddesses, and mythological narratives depicted with confident, celebratory energy. Sun imagery is an important aspect of this form.

Katchni — practised by the Kayastha community, is a more refined and linear style, using fine lines and cross-hatching to create texture and depth. The figures are delicate, the compositions intricate, the overall effect one of extraordinary precision and control.

Tantrik — rooted in the Tantric tradition, these paintings depict esoteric symbols, yantras, and the more powerful and complex aspects of the Hindu pantheon. They are among the most spiritually charged of all Madhubani works.

Godna — inspired by the tattoo tradition of the lower castes, Godna paintings use simple black lines on a plain ground to create compositions of striking directness and economy. They are among the most powerful and least embellished of all Madhubani styles.
Kohbar — the style specific to the bridal chamber, characterised by its central imagery of the lotus, the bamboo, and the fertility symbols that bless the new marriage.

The visual vocabulary of Madhubani is rich, specific, and deeply symbolic. The lotus, purity, fertility, and divine beauty. The fish, matsya, prosperity and abundance, sacred to the goddess. The bamboo grove, fertility and the continuity of life. The sun and moon, cosmic witnesses presiding over every composition. Serpents, protectors and symbols of the earth's power. Peacocks, beauty, love, and the coming of the rains. Elephants, wisdom and auspiciousness. Every motif carries meaning accumulated over centuries. Nothing is merely decorative.

Traditionally painted on freshly plastered mud walls using pigments drawn entirely from the natural world, turmeric for yellow, indigo for blue, cow dung and mud for earthy browns, kusum flowers for red, holi colours, soot and lamp black for the defining outlines. The brushes were twigs, bamboo sticks, fingers, and matchsticks. Today, Madhubani is also painted on paper, cloth, and canvas, a transition that has allowed the tradition to reach new audiences without losing the essential warmth and depth of its natural palette.

Madhubani is, at its heart, a tradition of prayer. Every painting is an offering, made at a moment of transition, celebration, gratitude, or supplication. The act of making is inseparable from the intention behind it. A woman painting the kohbar ghar is not simply decorating a room, she is invoking the blessings of the gods, the fertility of the earth, and the continuity of her family line. It is this understanding, that to paint is to pray, and that the image is alive with the intention that made it, that gives Madhubani its enduring power.

artforms.title: Phad
artforms.subtitle: Rajasthan · A 700-year-old scroll tradition
artforms.excerpt: A 700-year-old legacy originating in Shahpura, near Bhilwara, Rajasthan, Phad is one of India's most extraordinary scroll painting traditions, passed down with remarkable fidelity through generations of a single community of artists.
modalParagraphs: A 700-year-old legacy originating in Shahpura, near Bhilwara, Rajasthan, Phad is one of India's most extraordinary scroll painting traditions, passed down with remarkable fidelity through generations of a single community of artists.

Painted on cloth thirty feet long and five feet wide, each Phad narrates the religious stories of a local deity, most typically Devnarayanji, a reincarnation of Lord Vishnu, or Pabuji, the beloved local hero. Every inch of the cloth is filled with episodes from the deity's life, rendered in vibrant, jewel-bright colours that have remained essentially unchanged for centuries.

These paintings were not made to hang on walls. They were made to travel. Carried by priest-singers of the Rabari tribe, the Bhopas and their female counterparts, the Bhopis, Phads served as portable temples, bringing the divine into the villages of rural Rajasthan. After sunset, the scroll would be ceremonially unrolled, and the Bhopa would sing and perform the deity's stories through the night, illuminating each episode by lamplight as the narrative unfolded. Image and performance were inseparable, India's oldest form of illustrated storytelling.
The name itself tells the story. Phad means 'fold' in the local dialect, a reminder that these paintings lived their lives folded and carried, always in motion, always in service of community.

One of the most distinctive visual conventions of Phad painting is the way it renders character through portraiture. Every figure in the composition is shown in profile, with one telling exception. Villainous and negative characters are depicted with a full face, turned directly toward the viewer. In a tradition where the profile denotes virtue and heroism, the frontal gaze becomes a mark of moral corruption, a quietly brilliant visual language that allows even an illiterate audience to instantly read the ethical landscape of the story being told.

The making of a Phad is as ceremonial as its performance. Every element is completed before the most sacred detail is added last: the eyes of the main deity. Only then does the artwork come alive, transformed from painting into object of worship. The artist signs the work in close proximity to the deity, a gesture of both authorship and devotion.
Today, the Joshi family of Bhilwara remains the principal custodian of this living, seven-century tradition.

artforms.title: Pichwai
artforms.subtitle: Nathdwara, Rajasthan · Devotion in paint
artforms.excerpt: Pichwai is an art form of pure devotion and surrender, perhaps the most singularly dedicated of all India's painting traditions. Its etymology reveals its purpose entirely: pich, meaning behind, and wai, meaning one who belongs to, the painting that lives behind the deity, in service of the divine.
modalParagraphs: Pichwai is an art form of pure devotion and surrender, perhaps the most singularly dedicated of all India's painting traditions. Its etymology reveals its purpose entirely: pich, meaning behind, and wai, meaning one who belongs to, the painting that lives behind the deity, in service of the divine.

Pichwai belongs exclusively to the Nathdwara temple of Shrinathji in Rajasthan, the sacred shrine of the eight-year-old swaroop of Lord Krishna, depicted at the moment he lifted the Govardhan hill. It is, remarkably, the only art form in the world dedicated entirely to a single temple and a single deity. Every Pichwai ever made has been made for Shrinathji alone.

Traditionally, the Nathdwara Pichwai is blank at its centre, a deliberate absence that is in fact the composition's most important element. The painting adorns all sides with elaborate imagery, lotus, kadam trees, peacocks, devotees, and the symbols of Krishna's world, while the centre is left open so that the idol of Shrinathji, placed before it, becomes the painting's focal point. The Pichwai does not compete with the deity. It frames, celebrates, and surrenders to him.

Pichwai is not a single painting but a living liturgical calendar. There are twenty-four distinct variations, each corresponding to a specific darshan, festival, or season in the Nathdwara temple's devotional year. Summer Pichwais are painted on light, thin fabrics that breathe; winter brings heavy materials, velvets and brocades that carry the warmth of the season. Sharad Purnima, the full moon of autumn, calls for black silk, a dramatic, luminous ground against which the imagery of Krishna's moonlit Raas Leela shimmers with love and romance.

This responsiveness to season and festival makes Pichwai one of the most dynamic of all devotional art forms, not a fixed image but a living one, changing with the rhythms of the temple year, dressing the deity as one might dress a beloved child.
A distinct and lesser-known variant is Haveli ki Pichwai, paintings that depict the havelis of the sevadars of Shrinathji in Nathdwara, documenting the sacred domestic world surrounding the temple.

Perhaps the most profound aspect of Pichwai is what the artist chooses not to do. A Pichwai is never signed. In a tradition where the painting is understood as an offering to God rather than a work of personal expression, the artist's identity is surrendered along with the work itself. There is no authorship, no attribution, no individual claim.

artforms.title: Sanjhi
artforms.subtitle: Mathura · The golden hour of Braj
artforms.excerpt: The word Sanjhi derives from sanjh, or godhuli, the golden hour of dusk when cattle return home from grazing, their hooves raising clouds of dust in the fading light. It is the most beloved hour in the world of Braj, the hour when Krishna, the divine cowherd, would return to Vrindavan, and Radha would await him. Everything about this art form flows from that image.
modalParagraphs: The word Sanjhi derives from sanjh, or godhuli, the golden hour of dusk when cattle return home from grazing, their hooves raising clouds of dust in the fading light. It is the most beloved hour in the world of Braj, the hour when Krishna, the divine cowherd, would return to Vrindavan, and Radha would await him. Everything about this art form flows from that image.

Rooted entirely in the Leela of Radha and Krishna, their love, their play, their divine companionship in the groves and rivers of Vrindavan, Sanjhi is not merely devotional art. It is a daily act of longing, a visual offering made at the hour most associated with Krishna's return. Each composition is a meditation on a specific moment in the divine love story, the Raas Leela, the forests of Vrindavan, the Yamuna river, the Gopis, the peacocks and lotuses of the Braj landscape.

Sanjhi is created by cutting intricate designs into paper using specially crafted scissors of extraordinary precision, entirely freehand, guided by years of devoted practice. The beauty resides in the interplay of cut and uncut, presence and absence, light passing through paper as through a latticed screen.

A distinct and particularly poetic expression of the tradition is Jal Sanjhi, Sanjhi created on still water. Coloured, non-soluble powders are laid onto the water's surface with extraordinary care, forming intricate floating images of Krishna's world. Ephemeral even by the standards of a tradition that embraces impermanence, Jal Sanjhi exists only for the moment of its making.
The tradition reached its fullest flowering in the 16th and 17th centuries, when temple priests of the Braj region created Sanjhi compositions afresh each day during the festival season.

Sanjhi is the exclusive tradition of the Soni clan of Mathura, its guardians across generations, the community through whose hands this delicate and irreplaceable art has been kept alive in Krishna's own city.

artforms.title: Sohrai
artforms.subtitle: Jharkhand · A harvest tradition of the Santhal
artforms.excerpt: Sohrai is one of the finest and most purely preserved tribal art forms surviving in India, a tradition of extraordinary simplicity and integrity, created by the women of the Santhal community of Jharkhand in celebration of the harvest and in gratitude to the natural world that sustains them.
modalParagraphs: Sohrai is one of the finest and most purely preserved tribal art forms surviving in India, a tradition of extraordinary simplicity and integrity, created by the women of the Santhal community of Jharkhand in celebration of the harvest and in gratitude to the natural world that sustains them.

The art takes its name from the harvest festival it adorns, the most important celebration in the Santhal calendar, marking the end of the agricultural cycle. At this time, women paint the walls of their homes and on handmade paper, transforming the domestic space into a living expression of gratitude. The painting is not a record of the festival. It is the festival.

The tools are the simplest imaginable, twigs and sticks, shaped at their tips to create a flexible point. The colours are drawn entirely from nature, turmeric for yellow, henna for green and rust, charcoal for black. No manufactured pigments, no brushes, no preliminary sketches. The hand moves directly, guided by memory and years of practice.

Perhaps the most distinctive quality of Sohrai art is what it chooses not to depict. There are no human figures. In a tradition created by human hands to celebrate human life, the human form is entirely absent. Instead, the compositions are populated by livestock, insects, birds, and trees, the beings with whom the Santhal community shares its world, and upon whose wellbeing its own survival depends.

The forms are bold and direct, strong outlines, fluid lines, figures arranged with a rhythmic, instinctive balance. No perspective, no shadow, no naturalistic representation. These are not portraits but presences, archetypes of the living world, rendered with the confidence of a tradition that knows exactly what it wants to say.

Sohrai remains one of the most authentic expressions of tribal art in India, faithful to its materials, rooted in its community, and untouched in its essential vision by the pressures of the modern world.

artforms.title: Warli
artforms.subtitle: Maharashtra · The painted world of the Warli tribe
artforms.excerpt: Warli painting takes its name from the Warli tribe of Maharashtra, one of the largest and oldest tribal communities in India, living predominantly in the Dahanu, Palghar and Jawhar regions of Thane district. Remote, self-contained, and deeply rooted in the rhythms of the natural world, the Warli people developed a visual tradition as distinctive and coherent as any in India, a portrait of a community and its relationship with the living world around it.
modalParagraphs: Warli painting takes its name from the Warli tribe of Maharashtra, one of the largest and oldest tribal communities in India, living predominantly in the Dahanu, Palghar and Jawhar regions of Thane district. Remote, self-contained, and deeply rooted in the rhythms of the natural world, the Warli people developed a visual tradition as distinctive and coherent as any in India, one that is, at its heart, a portrait of a community and its relationship with the living world around it.

Like most tribal communities, the Warlis are pagan, their spirituality rooted not in scripture or institution but in the living forces of nature that surround them. Rain, sun, wind, the fertility of the earth, the turning of the seasons, each one is not merely a phenomenon but a presence, alive and deserving of reverence.

Warli paintings are created inside the home, on the interior walls of the mud hut. The wall is first smeared with a mixture of cow dung and mud, a base layer that smooths the surface and connects the act of painting to the organic materials of daily life. Over this, geru, red mud, is applied to create the characteristic warm terracotta ground against which the white figures will stand with such striking clarity. Today, when painted on paper or cloth, the base is still smeared with cow dung and/or geru mitti.

Being an agrarian community growing paddy, rice paste is used to create the figures. The brush is a pointed twig of the Bahari plant or bamboo, its tip chewed or split to create a fine, flexible point capable of the delicate line work that characterises the tradition.

The formal vocabulary of Warli painting is built from the simplest of geometric elements, the circle, the triangle, and the square. The circle represents the sun and moon, the cosmic and the cyclical. The triangle, derived from the pointed forms of mountains and trees, represents nature. The square denotes the sacred enclosure, the space set apart from the ordinary. From these three forms, in endlessly varied combination, the entire world of Warli painting is constructed. Figures are rendered as two triangles joined at their tips. The women are differentiated from men by a small hair bun. These figures dance, hunt, sow, harvest, marry, and celebrate, the full arc of community life depicted with a rhythmic vitality that gives Warli painting its characteristic sense of joyful, collective energy.

The central composition of the most important Warli paintings is the Chauk, a square sacred enclosure at the centre of which the Mother Goddess presides, surrounded by her devotees in concentric rings of figures and motifs. The Chauk is painted at weddings and harvest festivals, its creation an act of ritual as much as art. The tarpa (their local musical instrument), dance, the fishing net, the harvesting scene, nature in abundance, the household chores and depiction of daily life are the core of Warli art.

programmes.heading: A selection of past programmes
programmes.intro: Art Tree has long believed that art does not exist in isolation. Over the years we have curated a series of intimate baithaks and conversations, bringing together eminent historians, artists, musicians, chefs and cultural voices to explore the many dimensions of India's living heritage. These are not lectures. They are conversations: unhurried, curious and open.

cards.title: Delhi: Its Streets, Its Stories, Its Soul
cards.text: Seven conversations with the Dilliwalla historian and filmmaker, from the food that defines its neighbourhoods to the political theatre of the Red Fort, from clothing traditions to the quieter mohallas and markets. Scholarly and deeply personal.

cards.title: The Times and Life of Tawaifs
cards.withLabel: with Padma Shri Dr Rita Ganguly, Padma Shri Muzaffar Ali, Arshiya Sethi
cards.text: Three remarkable voices on the finest custodians of classical music, poetry and dance, the tawaifs who presided over mehfils and shaped the aesthetic culture of an era. A conversation as nuanced as it was necessary.

cards.title: Spice it Up: Flavours of Indian Cuisine
cards.withLabel: with Chef Manjit Gill, Gunjan Goela, Chef Bali, Chef Bhasin & Dr Pushpesh Pant
cards.text: Spice as history, identity and the thread that connects a civilisation across centuries of trade, migration and exchange. A series of conversations as rich, layered and full of surprise as the cuisine they explored.
